frontMatter.title: Etymology
paragraphs: (Supplied by a Late Consumptive Usher to a Grammar School.)

The pale Usher — threadbare in coat, heart, body, and brain; I can see him now. He was always dusting his old dictionaries and grammars with an odd handkerchief, mockingly decorated with all the bright flags of all the known nations of the world. He loved to dust his old grammars; somehow it mildly reminded him of his mortality.

"When you take it upon yourselves to school others, and to teach them what a whale-fish is to be called in our language, and through ignorance leave out the letter H, which almost by itself makes up the meaning of the word, you are teaching what is not true." — Hackluyt.
"WHALE. * * * Swedish and Danish hval. This animal is named from roundness or rolling; for in Danish hvalt means arched or vaulted." — Webster's Dictionary.
"WHALE. * * * It comes more directly from the Dutch and German Wallen; Anglo-Saxon Walw-ian, to roll, to wallow." — Richardson's Dictionary.

‏חו‎, Hebrew. ϰητος, Greek. CETUS, Latin. WHŒL, Anglo-Saxon. HVALT, Danish. WAL, Dutch. HWAL, Swedish. HVALUR, Icelandic. WHALE, English. BALEINE, French. BALLENA, Spanish. PEKEE-NUEE-NUEE, Fijian. PEHEE-NUEE-NUEE, Erromangoan.

frontMatter.title: Extracts
paragraphs: (Supplied by a Sub-Sub-Librarian).

You will see that this mere painstaking burrower and grub-worm of a poor devil of a Sub-Sub seems to have gone through the long Vaticans and street-stalls of the earth, picking up whatever random allusions to whales he could find anywhere, in any book whatsoever, sacred or profane. So you must not, in every case at least, take the higgledy-piggledy whale statements in these extracts, however authentic, as genuine gospel cetology. Far from it. As for the ancient authors in general, and the poets who appear here as well, these extracts are valuable or entertaining only because they offer a glancing bird's-eye view of what has been said, thought, imagined, and sung about Leviathan, indiscriminately, by many nations and generations, including our own.

So farewell, poor devil of a Sub-Sub, whose commentator I am. You belong to that hopeless, sallow tribe that no wine in this world will ever warm, and for whom even Pale Sherry would be too rosy-strong; but with whom one sometimes loves to sit, and feel poor-devilish too, and grow convivial over tears, and say to them bluntly, with full eyes and empty glasses, and in a sadness not altogether unpleasant — Give it up, Sub-Subs! For the more pains you take to please the world, the more thankless you will go forever! I wish I could clear out Hampton Court and the Tuileries for you! But gulp down your tears and hurry aloft to the royal-mast with your hearts; for your friends who have gone before are clearing out the seven-storied heavens, and making refugees of long-pampered Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael, in readiness for your coming. Here you strike only splintered hearts together — there, you shall strike unsplinterable glasses!
EXTRACTS.
"And God created great whales." — Genesis.
"Leviathan maketh a path to shine after him; One would think the deep to be hoary." — Job.
"Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah." — Jonah.
"There go the ships; there is that Leviathan whom thou hast made to play therein." — Psalms.

"In that day, the Lord with his sore, and great, and strong sword, shall punish Leviathan the piercing serpent, even Leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea." — Isaiah.

"And whatever else comes within the chaos of this monster's mouth, be it beast, boat, or stone, down it all goes, unchecked, through that foul great gullet of his, and perishes in the bottomless gulf of his belly." — Holland's Plutarch's Morals.

"The Indian Sea breeds the most and the biggest fish there are: among them the Whales and Whirlpools called Balaene, which take up as much in length as four acres or arpents of land." — Holland's Pliny.

"We had hardly been two days at sea when, about sunrise, a great many whales and other sea monsters appeared. Among the former, one was of a most monstrous size.... It came toward us open-mouthed, raising the waves on every side and beating the sea ahead of it into foam." — Tooke's Lucian. "The True History."

"He also visited this country with a view to catching horse-whales, which had bones of very great value for their teeth, some of which he brought to the king.... The best whales were caught in his own country, some of them forty-eight and some fifty yards long. He said that he was one of six who had killed sixty in two days." — Other or Octher's verbal narrative taken down from his mouth by King Alfred, A.D. 890.

"And whereas everything else, whether beast or vessel, that enters the dreadful gulf of this monster's (whale's) mouth is immediately lost and swallowed up, the sea-gudgeon retreats into it in great security, and sleeps there." — MONTAIGNE. — Apology for Raimond Sebond.
"Let's run, let's run! Old Nick take me if this isn't Leviathan, described by the noble prophet Moses in the life of patient Job." — Rabelais.
"This whale's liver was two cartloads." — Stowe's Annals.
"The great Leviathan that maketh the seas to seethe like boiling pan." — Lord Bacon's Version of the Psalms.

"As for that monstrous bulk of the whale or ork, we have received nothing certain. They grow extremely fat, so much so that an incredible quantity of oil can be extracted from a single whale." — Ibid. "History of Life and Death."
"The sovereignest thing on earth is parmacetti for an inward bruise." — King Henry.
"Very like a whale." — Hamlet.

"Which to secure, no skill of leech's art Mote him avail, but to return again To his wound's worker, that with lowly dart, Dinting his breast, had bred his restless pain, Like as the wounded whale to shore flies thro' the main." — The Fairie Queen.
"As immense as whales, the motion of whose vast bodies can, in a peaceful calm, trouble the ocean until it boils." — Sir William Davenant. Preface to Gondibert.

"What spermaceti is, men might well doubt, since the learned Hosmannus, in his work of thirty years, says plainly, Nescio quid sit (I do not know what it is)." — Sir T. Browne. Of Sperma Ceti and the Sperma Ceti Whale. Vide his V. E.

"Like Spencer's Talus with his modern flail He threatens ruin with his ponderous tail. ... Their fixed jav'lins in his side he wears, And on his back a grove of pikes appears." — Waller's Battle of the Summer Islands.
"By art that great Leviathan is created, called a Commonwealth or State — (in Latin, Civitas) which is nothing but an artificial man." — Opening sentence of Hobbes's Leviathan.
"Silly Mansoul swallowed it without chewing, as if it had been a sprat in the mouth of a whale." — Pilgrim's Progress.
"That sea beast Leviathan, which God of all his works Created hugest that swim the ocean stream." — Paradise Lost.

— "There Leviathan, Hugest of living creatures, in the deep Stretched like a promontory sleeps or swims, And seems a moving land; and at his gills Draws in, and at his breath spouts out a sea." — Ibid.
"The mighty whales that swim in a sea of water, and have a sea of oil swimming in them." — Fuller's Profane and Holy State.
"So close behind some promontory lie The huge Leviathan to attend their prey, And give no chance, but swallow in the fry, Which through their gaping jaws mistake the way." — Dryden's Annus Mirabilis.

"While the whale is floating at the ship's stern, they cut off his head and tow it with a boat as near the shore as it will come; but it will run aground in twelve or thirteen feet of water." — Thomas Edge's Ten Voyages to Spitzbergen, in Purchas.

"On their way they saw many whales sporting in the ocean, and in sheer playfulness fuzzing up the water through their pipes and vents, which nature has placed on their shoulders." — Sir T. Herbert's Voyages into Asia and Africa. Harris Coll.
"Here they saw such huge troops of whales that they were forced to proceed with a great deal of caution, for fear of running their ship onto them." — Schouten's Sixth Circumnavigation.

"We set sail from the Elbe, wind N.E., in the ship called The Jonas-in-the-Whale.... Some say the whale can't open his mouth, but that is a fable.... They often climb up the masts to see whether they can spot a whale, for the first to discover one gets a ducat for his pains.... I was told of a whale taken near Shetland that had more than a barrel of herrings in his belly.... One of our harpooners told me that he once caught a whale in Spitzbergen that was white all over." — A Voyage to Greenland, A.D. 1671. Harris Coll.

"Several whales have come in on this coast (Fife) in the year 1652; one of the whalebone kind, eighty feet long, came in, which (as I was informed), besides a vast quantity of oil, yielded 500 weight of baleen. Its jaws stand as a gate in the garden of Pitferren." — Sibbald's Fife and Kinross.

"I myself have agreed to try whether I can master and kill this spermaceti whale, for I have never heard of any of that kind being killed by any man, such is his fierceness and swiftness." — Richard Strafford's Letter from the Bermudas. Phil. Trans. A.D. 1668.
"Whales in the sea God's voice obey." — N. E. Primer.

"We also saw an abundance of large whales, there being more in those southern seas, I might say, by a hundred to one, than we have to the north of us." — Captain Cowley's Voyage round the Globe, A.D. 1729.
"... and the whale's breath is often accompanied by so unbearable a smell as to bring on a disorder of the brain." — Ulloa's South America.

"To fifty chosen sylphs of special note, We trust the important charge, the petticoat. Oft have we known that seven-fold fence to fail, Tho' stuffed with hoops and armed with ribs of whale." — Rape of the Lock.

"If we compare land animals in size with those that make their home in the deep, we shall find they look contemptible by comparison. The whale is doubtless the largest animal in creation." — Goldsmith, Nat. Hist.
"If you were to write a fable for little fishes, you would make them talk like great whales." — Goldsmith to Johnson.

"In the afternoon we saw what was taken to be a rock, but it turned out to be a dead whale, which some Asiatics had killed and were then towing ashore. They seemed to be trying to hide behind the whale, so as not to be seen by us." — Cook's Voyages.

"They seldom venture to attack the larger whales. They stand in such great dread of some of them that, when out at sea, they are afraid even to mention their names, and they carry dung, limestone, juniper wood, and some other articles of the same kind in their boats, to frighten them and keep them from coming too near." — Uno Von Troil's Letters on Banks's and Solander's Voyage to Iceland in 1772.

"The Spermaceti Whale found by the Nantuckois is an active, fierce animal, and calls for great skill and boldness in the fishermen." — Thomas Jefferson's Whale Memorial to the French minister in 1778.
"And tell me, sir, what in the world is equal to it?" — Edmund Burke's reference in Parliament to the Nantucket Whale-Fishery.
"Spain — a great whale stranded on the shores of Europe." — Edmund Burke. (somewhere.)

"A tenth branch of the king's ordinary revenue, said to be founded on the grounds that he guards and protects the seas from pirates and robbers, is the right to royal fish, which are whale and sturgeon. And these, whether thrown ashore or caught near the coast, are the property of the king." — Blackstone.
"Soon to the sport of death the crews repair: Rodmond unerring o'er his head suspends The barbed steel, and every turn attends." — Falconer's Shipwreck.
"Bright shone the roofs, the domes, the spires, And rockets blew self driven, To hang their momentary fire Around the vault of heaven.
"So fire with water to compare, The ocean serves on high, Up-spouted by a whale in air, To express unwieldy joy." — Cowper, on the Queen's Visit to London.
"Ten or fifteen gallons of blood are thrown out of the heart at a single stroke, with immense velocity." — John Hunter's account of the dissection of a whale. (A small-sized one.)

"The aorta of a whale is wider in bore than the main pipe of the waterworks at London Bridge, and the water roaring through that pipe has less force and speed than the blood gushing from the whale's heart." — Paley's Theology.
"The whale is a mammal without hind feet." — Baron Cuvier.

"At 40 degrees south we saw Spermaceti Whales, but did not catch any until the first of May, when the sea was covered with them." — Colnett's Voyage for the Purpose of Extending the Spermacetti Whale Fishery.

"In the free element beneath me swam, Floundered and dived, in play, in chase, in battle, Fishes of every color, form, and kind; Which language cannot paint, and mariner Had never seen; from dread Leviathan To insect millions peopling every wave: Gather'd in shoals immense, like floating islands, Led by mysterious instincts through that waste And trackless region, though on every side Assaulted by voracious enemies, Whales, sharks, and monsters, arm'd in front or jaw, With swords, saws, spiral horns, or hooked fangs." — Montgomery's World before the Flood.

"Io! Paean! Io! sing. To the finny people's king. Not a mightier whale than this In the vast Atlantic is; Not a fatter fish than he, Flounders round the Polar Sea." — Charles Lamb's Triumph of the Whale.

"In the year 1690 some people were on a high hill watching the whales spouting and sporting with each other, when one of them remarked: there — pointing to the sea — is a green pasture where our children's grandchildren will go for bread." — Obed Macy's History of Nantucket.
"I built a cottage for Susan and myself and made a gateway in the shape of a Gothic arch by setting up a whale's jawbones." — Hawthorne's Twice Told Tales.
"She came to order a monument for her first love, who had been killed by a whale in the Pacific Ocean no less than forty years ago." — Ibid.
"No, sir, it's a Right Whale," answered Tom. "I saw his spout; he threw up a pair of rainbows as pretty as any Christian would wish to look at. He's a raal oil-butt, that fellow!" — Cooper's Pilot.
"The papers were brought in, and we saw in the Berlin Gazette that whales had been brought onto the stage there." — Eckermann's Conversations with Goethe.

"My God! Mr. Chace, what is the matter?" I answered, "We have been stove in by a whale." — "Narrative of the Shipwreck of the Whale Ship Essex of Nantucket, which was attacked and finally destroyed by a large Sperm Whale in the Pacific Ocean." By Owen Chace of Nantucket, first mate of said vessel. New York, 1821.

"A mariner sat in the shrouds one night, The wind was piping free; Now bright, now dimmed, was the moonlight pale, And the phosphor gleamed in the wake of the whale, As it floundered in the sea." — Elizabeth Oakes Smith.
"The quantity of line drawn out of the boats engaged in capturing this one whale came altogether to 10,440 yards, or nearly six English miles....
"Sometimes the whale shakes its tremendous tail in the air, and it cracks like a whip and resounds for a distance of three or four miles." — Scoresby.

"Maddened by the agonies he suffers from these fresh attacks, the infuriated Sperm Whale rolls over and over; he rears his enormous head and, with jaws spread wide, snaps at everything around him; he rushes at the boats with his head; they are driven before him with great speed, and sometimes completely destroyed.... It is a matter of great astonishment that the study of the habits of so interesting and, commercially, so important an animal (as the Sperm Whale) should have been so entirely neglected, or should have aroused so little curiosity among the numerous observers, many of them competent, who in recent years must have had the most abundant and most convenient opportunities to witness its habits." — Thomas Beale's History of the Sperm Whale, 1839.

"The Cachalot" (Sperm Whale) "is not only better armed than the True Whale" (Greenland or Right Whale) "in having a formidable weapon at each end of its body, but also more often shows a disposition to use these weapons offensively, and in a manner at once so cunning, bold and mischievous, that it has come to be regarded as the most dangerous to attack of all the known species of the whale tribe." — Frederick Debell Bennett's Whaling Voyage Round the Globe, 1840.

October 13. "There she blows," was sung out from the masthead. "Where away?" demanded the captain. "Three points off the lee bow, sir." "Raise up your wheel. Steady!" "Steady, sir." "Masthead ahoy! Do you see that whale now?" "Aye aye, sir! A school of Sperm Whales! There she blows! There she breaches!" "Sing out! Sing out every time!" "Aye aye, sir! There she blows! There — there — thar she blows — bowes — bo-o-os!" "How far off?" "Two and a half miles." "Thunder and lightning! So near! Call all hands." — J. Ross Browne's Etchings of a Whaling Cruize. 1846.

"The whale-ship Globe, on board which the horrible events we are about to relate took place, belonged to the island of Nantucket." — "Narrative of the Globe Mutiny," by Lay and Hussey survivors. A.D. 1828.

Once, when he was being pursued by a whale he had wounded, he fended off its attack for some time with a lance; but the furious monster finally rushed on the boat, and he and his comrades were saved only by leaping into the water when they saw the onset could not be avoided." — Missionary Journal of Tyerman and Bennett.

"Nantucket itself," said Mr. Webster, "is a very striking and distinctive part of the national interest. There is a population of eight or nine thousand people living here in the sea, adding greatly every year to the national wealth through the boldest and most persevering industry." — Report of Daniel Webster's Speech in the U. S. Senate, on the application for the Erection of a Breakwater at Nantucket. 1828.

"The whale fell directly on top of him, and probably killed him instantly." — "The Whale and his Captors, or The Whaleman's Adventures and the Whale's Biography, gathered on the Homeward Cruise of the Commodore Preble." By Rev. Henry T. Cheever.

"If you make the least damn bit of noise," replied Samuel, "I will send you to hell." — Life of Samuel Comstock (the mutineer), by his brother, William Comstock. Another Version of the whale-ship Globe narrative.

"The voyages of the Dutch and English to the Northern Ocean, made in the hope of discovering a passage through it to India, failed in their main object but laid open the haunts of the whale." — McCulloch's Commercial Dictionary.

"These things are reciprocal; the ball rebounds only to bound forward again; for now, in laying open the haunts of the whale, the whalemen seem to have indirectly hit upon new clues to that same mystic North-West Passage." — From "Something" unpublished.

"It is impossible to meet a whale-ship on the ocean without being struck by how she looks up close. The vessel under short sail, with lookouts at the mastheads eagerly scanning the wide expanse around them, has an entirely different air from ships engaged on a regular voyage." — Currents and Whaling. U.S. Ex. Ex.

"Walkers around London and elsewhere may remember having seen large curved bones set upright in the ground, either to form arches over gateways or entrances to alcoves, and they may perhaps have been told that these were the ribs of whales." — Tales of a Whale Voyager to the Arctic Ocean.

"It was not until the boats returned from chasing these whales that the whites saw their ship in the bloody possession of the savages who had been signed on among the crew." — Newspaper Account of the Taking and Retaking of the Whale-Ship Hobomack.
"It is generally well known that, of the crews of whaling vessels (American), few ever return in the ships they sailed out on." — Cruise in a Whale Boat.
"Suddenly a mighty mass rose out of the water and shot straight up into the air. It was the whale." — Miriam Coffin or the Whale Fisherman.
"The Whale is harpooned, to be sure; but just think how you would manage a powerful unbroken colt with nothing but a rope tied to the root of his tail." — A Chapter on Whaling in Ribs and Trucks.

"On one occasion I saw two of these monsters (whales), probably male and female, swimming slowly one after the other, less than a stone's throw from the shore" (Tierra del Fuego), "over which the beech tree spread its branches." — Darwin's Voyage of a Naturalist.

"'Stern all!' shouted the mate as, turning his head, he saw the gaping jaws of a large Sperm Whale close to the bow of the boat, threatening it with instant destruction — 'Stern all, for your lives!'" — Wharton the Whale Killer.
"So be cheery, my lads, let your hearts never fail, While the bold harpooner is striking the whale!" — Nantucket Song.
"Oh, the rare old Whale, mid storm and gale In his ocean home will be A giant in might, where might is right, And King of the boundless sea." — Whale Song.
